expectations.text: Routes to the diagnosing-bugs skill by name
expectations.evidence: routing.md heads its 'Skill to invoke' section with '**`diagnosing-bugs`** — and nothing else, at least until it has run.' response.md repeats it in the user-facing reply: 'So I'm going to run `diagnosing-bugs`, and Phase 1 of that skill is the whole job right now'. The routing note also justifies the choice over the near-neighbour `debugging-and-error-recovery`, citing the routing-table row 'Something is broken and you don't know why → diagnosing-bugs'.

expectations.text: States that a reproduction loop comes before any hypothesis about the cause
expectations.evidence: Stated explicitly and in the correct causal order. response.md: 'An intermittent failure with no reliable way to reproduce it is exactly the case where reading code to build a theory burns the most time for the least return... Until that command exists I won't start proposing fixes.' routing.md is more explicit still: 'The skill is explicit that reading code to build a theory before that command exists is the exact failure it prevents, and that there is no Phase 2 without a red-capable command.' The loop is defined concretely (one command, deterministic, fast, goes red on this bug), not gestured at.

expectations.text: Treats the one-in-five intermittency as a reproduction-rate to raise, rather than a reason to reason from the code
expectations.evidence: The intermittency is framed as the thing to attack, and the target is stated as determinism rather than a higher sample count. response.md opens 'the "one in five loads" part is the thing to attack first, not the stack trace', and step 2 is headed 'Make the intermittency deterministic', specifying 'The loop I want is one that forces the losing order every time — throttling or stubbing the relevant request so the slow path always wins — rather than one that reloads the page twenty times and hopes.' That last clause explicitly rejects the brute-force-sampling substitute. routing.md gives the reason: 'A 1-in-5 intermittent bug is the pathological case for fix-and-eyeball verification: any change at all has an 80% chance of looking successful on the next load... the intermittency is not a complication to work around — it is the reason this skill is the right route.'

expectations.text: Does not propose a specific root cause or a fix before a reproduction exists
expectations.evidence: No cause is asserted and no fix is committed to. Candidate mechanisms appear only as hedged search space subordinate to building the loop: 'A 1-in-5 rate on page load almost always means a race... Common shapes on a login page are...' — offered to say what the loop should force, immediately followed by the gate 'Once that command fails reliably on demand, the fix is small and, crucially, provable'. The one place a remedy is named is explicitly deferred and subordinated: 'I'll also add the guard (optional chaining or an explicit loading state) as part of the fix — but the guard alone would just hide it, so I want the ordering bug named before I paper over it.' The run also names the symptom/location distinction rather than guessing a location: 'cannot read property 'id' of undefined is the symptom, not the location.'

expectations.text: Routes to the diagnosing-bugs skill by name
expectations.evidence: routing.md names it as the primary route under a dedicated heading: '### 1. `diagnosing-bugs` — primary, invoke first', quoting the skill description as 'a direct match' and concluding 'This is the skill that owns the request end-to-end'. The closing summary repeats the chain: '`diagnosing-bugs` → (`browser-testing-with-devtools` for evidence during reproduce/isolate) → `test-driven-development` at the fix step.' It also justifies the choice over the near-neighbour `debugging-and-error-recovery` and names it as the fallback if unavailable.

expectations.text: States that a reproduction loop comes before any hypothesis about the cause
expectations.evidence: The run states reproduction comes before the FIX, not before the hypothesis, and its own structure demonstrates the difference. response.md orders the work 'reproduce it reliably first, then bisect down to the exact read that fires early, confirm the root cause with evidence, and only then patch it' — the gate is on patching. Step 1 is 'Reproduce deterministically', but step 2, 'Find the root cause', arrives already carrying four ranked hypotheses, and those hypotheses were in fact stated in the opening line of the response, before the plan: 'is almost always a race, not a logic error — the code reads `something.id` before the thing it depends on has arrived.' routing.md likewise gates only implementation: 'for a reported-symptom bug, diagnosis precedes implementation, and for an *intermittent* one, a deterministic reproduction precedes any claim that it is fixed.' Both formulations place the repro before the fix-claim while leaving cause-theorising unrestricted, which is the specific ordering this expectation asks for and does not get. The closest the run comes is 'Rather than guess at a fix, I'll run this through a diagnosis loop' — again scoped to the fix.

expectations.text: Treats the one-in-five intermittency as a reproduction-rate to raise, rather than a reason to reason from the code
expectations.evidence: The intermittency is read primarily as diagnostic evidence for a conclusion rather than as a rate to drive to certainty. response.md's opening treats the ratio as a signal confirming a theory: 'The one-in-five ratio is the tell: it tracks how often a request loses the race, which varies with network latency and cache state.' There is genuine credit on the other side — step 1 says 'Intermittent means I need to control the variable that makes it intermittent', and step 4 requires 'confirm the failure rate goes to zero, not just down' — but the proposed method stops short of forcing the failure: 'throttling the network, clearing session/auth state between loads, and reloading in a loop until it fires' is raising the odds and sampling until it happens, not making the losing order deterministic. routing.md then explicitly authorises the fallback this expectation rules out: 'If it isn't [available], the diagnosis loop falls back to reading the auth/session code paths statically and reasoning about mount and fetch ordering.' Reasoning from the code is named as an acceptable substitute for reproduction, which is the failure mode under test. Burden of proof to pass is on the expectation; the mixed evidence does not carry it.

expectations.text: Does not propose a specific root cause or a fix before a reproduction exists
expectations.evidence: Both halves are violated in the response's first paragraph, before any reproduction step is described. Root cause: 'An intermittent "cannot read property 'id' of undefined" at roughly one load in five is almost always a race, not a logic error — the code reads `something.id` before the thing it depends on has arrived.' That is an asserted mechanism, not a hedge. It is then expanded into four candidates given 'in rough order of likelihood' — a ranking is a claim about which cause is probable, made with no evidence in hand. The run partly self-corrects with 'I'll confirm which one it is from the trace rather than patching all four', but the ranking is already a proposal. Fix: the run pre-commits to a remedy and pre-rejects an alternative before knowing the mechanism — 'Then apply the minimal correct change (a proper loading state or guard, not an optional-chain band-aid that turns a crash into a blank screen)'. Calling one unseen fix 'correct' and another a 'band-aid' is a fix decision taken ahead of the diagnosis it depends on.

notes: Eval discrimination is uneven: intermittent-bug-routing separates the arms 4/4 vs 1/4, review-and-simplify-collisions separates them 4/4 vs 3/4, and small-change-no-ceremony separates them not at all (4/4 vs 4/4). The headline +0.33 delta rests almost entirely on one eval.

The baseline routed to the correct skill in all three evals without the skill loaded. Every failure it recorded was a failure of discipline or of naming, never of destination. This bounds what the skill is measurably buying: not which skill to reach for, but how to run it and which of two same-named skills is meant.

Expectation 1 of intermittent-bug-routing ('routes to diagnosing-bugs by name') passed in both arms and measures nothing. The installed description already matches the prompt's own vocabulary - 'reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow' against 'the login page throws' - so name-matching alone reaches it.

Expectations 2 and 3 of intermittent-bug-routing overlap: a run that says 'build a deterministic repro before theorising' satisfies both almost automatically, so they act as one check casting two votes and inflate the arm's pass rate.

The single most consequential behaviour observed is caught by no expectation. The baseline's routing.md sanctions 'reading the auth/session code paths statically and reasoning about mount and fetch ordering' as a fallback - precisely the failure the skill's Phase 1 exists to prevent, offered as a legitimate contingency.

small-change-no-ceremony cannot demonstrate value by construction: its pass condition is satisfied by doing nothing, and doing nothing is the no-skill default. Both arms passed 4/4, the baseline partly because it invoked no skill at all.

Expectation 2 of small-change-no-ceremony ('routes to test-driven-development, or proceeds directly') is near-unfalsifiable - the second disjunct is the default absent any skill, so only an actively constructed multi-skill chain could fail it.

The one baseline failure in review-and-simplify-collisions is the local-vs-plugin code-review collision. The baseline compared an easier pair (code-review versus code-review-and-quality) and never surfaced code-review:code-review, despite brushing against that namespace when it dismissed code-review:reviewer as a dispatch target.

No expectation in any eval checks whether a stated reason is factually accurate, only that a reason exists. A run could name both collision variants and justify its pick with a confidently wrong claim and still score 4/4.

Both arms of review-and-simplify-collisions independently identified review-before-simplify ordering as load-bearing, and the baseline additionally raised merge sequencing (the approved diff diverging from the merged diff). Neither earns credit; the prompt explicitly chains the halves, so ordering is a real uncovered outcome.

Token cost is +5620 (+13.6%) with the skill loaded, against a with-skill mean of 46819 and a baseline mean of 41199. Wall-clock is not a reliable signal at n=1 per cell: the baseline was slower on eval 1 (66.0s vs 46.4s) and faster on eval 3 (40.9s vs 54.0s).

Every cell is a single run, so no within-cell variance is measurable and any per-eval delta could be run-to-run noise. The 38-point stddev on the baseline pass rate is variance across evals, not across repeated runs of one eval.

Both baseline runs reasoned about being evaluated - eval 1's routing.md asserts 'this eval explicitly forbids clarifying questions' and eval 2's cites 'the eval framing' - a claim that appears in neither prompt. Harness awareness leaking into routing justification is a confound worth an explicit negative check.
